Calophysus macropterus, commonly known as the zamurito, exhibits a life history strategy typical of many large-bodied Amazonian catfishes. Neonates emerge from the egg at a remarkably small size, with newly hatched larvae weighing only approximately 0.0028 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0028 grams], a value that reflects the limited yolk reserves available at the end of embryonic development. This initial mass is among the smallest recorded for pimelodid catfishes, likely an adaptation linked to the production of numerous small eggs. Field studies conducted under controlled thermal regimes indicate that embryonic development proceeds rapidly at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], with hatching occurring after just about 5 days [ab = just about 5 days]. These early life stages are thus extremely brief, and the small size at birth imposes a high vulnerability to starvation and predation during the initial transition to exogenous feeding.

As the zamurito grows, size at reproductive maturation differs markedly between the sexes, a pattern commonly observed in siluriform fishes. Females attain puberty at a total length of 27 centimeters [Lp = 27 centimeters], whereas males reach sexual maturity at a somewhat smaller body size of 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation length suggests that females require additional somatic growth to accommodate the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and egg production. At the point of puberty, females typically weigh approximately 195.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 195.7 grams], a mass that correlates well with the length-based threshold. These values were derived from extensive field sampling across the Amazon basin and are consistent across several surveyed populations, indicating a relatively canalized maturation schedule under natural conditions.

Beyond the size at maturation, the species achieves a substantial ultimate body size, with individuals reaching a maximum recorded total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters]. The corresponding asymptotic mass for adults is considerable, with large specimens attaining an ultimate wet weight of 664.5 grams [Wwi = 664.5 grams], reflecting the robust, deep-bodied morphology characteristic of this predatory catfish. This maximum body mass is achieved over a relatively long lifespan; available data suggest that individuals may live for as long as 15 years [am = 15 years] under the stable thermal conditions of the Amazon floodplain, with a mean annual water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Such longevity is typical of slow-growing, apex piscivores that occupy a high trophic position within the varzea ecosystem.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female zamurito has been quantified through histological and gravimetric analysis of gonadal tissue. During the peak of the spawning season, the gonadosomatic index for mature females reached 20% [GSI = 20%] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This measurement was obtained from fish held in river enclosures at the ambient water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] during the rising-water period, when vitellogenic activity is maximal.

From a comparative perspective, the life-history traits of Calophysus macropterus align with a K-selected strategy, characterized by delayed reproduction, slow growth to a large ultimate size, and extended longevity. The ontogenetic trajectory from the initial mass recorded at hatching of about 0.0028 grams [Wwb = about 0.0028 grams] to the adult asymptotic mass of 664.5 grams [Wwi = 664.5 grams] represents a roughly 240,000-fold increase in wet weight, a striking physiological expansion that demands prolonged juvenile development before first breeding. This pattern stands in contrast to many smaller Amazonian characiforms, which mature rapidly and have short lifespans. The relatively advanced age at first reproduction in zamurito, coupled with the moderate gonadal investment and large body size, reflects an evolutionary response to the predictable but seasonally pulsed productivity of the whitewater floodplains it inhabits.
